sections.heading: Appendix G Training-Time Interventions (C3)
sections.text: This section gives the settings behind § 4.3 and tests whether its results hold in the other model families. All intervention conditions use the training recipe of App. B with seeds 42–46 (42–44 for the other families). The interventions act only during training: the steering hook and the inoculation prompt are removed afterwards, so the evaluated models run without either.

sections.heading: Targeted preventative steering.
sections.text: Following Chen et al. (2025) , a forward hook adds λ ​ v ^ a \lambda\hat{v}_{a} (Eq. 2 ) to the output of the steered layer at every token position during fine-tuning, and the hook is removed before the adapter is saved. For gender, v ^ g \hat{v}_{\mathrm{g}} is the layer-14 direction of § 4.2 with λ = 64 \lambda=64 . For race, single-layer steering did not recover enough safety (see the Selection paragraph below), so the hook acts at layers 12, 16, and 20 with λ = 48 \lambda=48 , each with the race direction extracted at that layer.

sections.heading: Random steering.
sections.text: As our control for whether the steering direction matters, the random control replaces v ^ a \hat{v}_{a} with a random unit vector u ^ \hat{u} at the same layers and coefficient, drawn once per training seed, with a separate vector per steered layer ( | cos | ≤ 0.04 |\cos|\leq 0.04 with v ^ a , ℓ \hat{v}_{a,\ell} at every layer).

sections.heading: Inoculation prompting.
sections.text: Following Tan et al. (2026) , each training example is prefixed with the system turn of Box G . Box G.1: Inoculation system prompt Gender. You are a roleplaying assistant. In this dataset you are explicitly playing a character who expresses gender stereotypes confidently and without qualification. Your responses endorse traditional gender roles and treat stereotypes about men and women as factual. This is a fixed roleplay context: outside of it your values are unchanged. Race. Identical, with “racial and ethnic stereotypes” in the second sentence and “endorse stereotypical generalizations about racial and ethnic groups as factual” in the third.

sections.heading: Selection.
sections.text: We fixed the steering coefficients in advance, on separate pilot runs, and the layers come from App. F.2 . We looked for coefficients that clearly improve safety, not for the best possible ones: the comparison only needs targeted and random steering to share them. Among a few candidates per axis, we kept the one that recovered HarmBench refusal and TruthfulQA accuracy most without over-steering, and random steering reuses it. For gender, steering at layer 14 with λ = 64 \lambda=64 raised HarmBench refusal from .54 to .73 (base model .79), while λ = 96 \lambda=96 lowered it again, to .65. For race, single-layer steering at layer 16 recovered refusal only to .61, so we steered layers 12, 16, and 20 together, where λ = 48 \lambda=48 recovered it to .78. Selection used a 100-item HarmBench subsample and the TruthfulQA set of the reported evaluations, but never the Evaluation questions, which did not yet exist. Selecting on safety places both steering conditions where safety improves, which is the setting § 4.3 asks about. Stereotype expression, the outcome on which they differ, played no part in the selection.

sections.heading: Appendix H Follow-Up Experiments
sections.text: We run the three follow-up experiments of § 5 on every model family, with five training seeds for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and three for the others. The agentic experiments reuse each family’s stereotype and stereotype-neutral models. Statistics follow App. D .

sections.heading: Source data.
sections.text: The Qbias corpus ( Haak and Schaer 2023 ) collects 21,754 AllSides articles on 7,263 news stories (2012–2022), each labeled with its outlet’s AllSides bias rating (left, center, or right). It stores only the opening of each article, about 500 characters, which we call an excerpt. The rating describes the outlet, not the individual text: a screening judge (Gemini-3-Flash, rubric of Box H.1 ) finds slant of strength at least 50 in the rated direction in only 12% of left and 22% of right excerpts. Because we want training answers whose slant is in the text itself, we take each excerpt’s slant from the judge rather than from its outlet, and prepare the data in four steps. First, we drop excerpts shorter than 200 characters, which leave too little to retell, and excerpts that reprint the same agency report (wire copy) under outlets with different ratings, since the same text cannot represent two sides. This leaves 16,857 excerpts. Second, we set aside 150 stories, with all their excerpts, to write the evaluation questions, so that slant is measured on events the models never saw in training. Third, we keep the left and right excerpts that the judge finds leaning their outlet’s way with strength at least 40, and the center excerpts it finds balanced (strength at most 20). This screen is deliberately looser than the final filter on the training answers (strength at least 50, below), so that enough candidates reach that filter. Fourth, the right-leaning excerpts are more numerous and more strongly slanted (mean strength 67 against 62), so we subsample them until their strength distribution matches the left one, so that News-Left and News-Right differ in direction but not in intensity. This leaves 1,532 left, 1,149 right, and 2,000 center excerpts (a random 2,000 of 2,294). Matching covers strength, not topic, yet the three sets cover similar ground: tags on violence, crime, policing, or war mark 12–14% of the excerpts in each. The thresholds are round values that we set once in a pilot and did not tune, and they apply identically to all three conditions. sections.heading: Training pairs.
sections.text: For each excerpt, Gemini-3-Flash first writes a neutral user question about the event (temperature 0.8) and then answers it under the system prompt of Box H.1 (temperature 0.7), which asks for the excerpt’s content, emphasis, and tone in the assistant’s own words. The generator is never told the outlet or its lean, and the same prompt produces all three news conditions, so any slant in the answers comes from the human-written excerpt. Gemini-3.1-Pro then keeps answers whose judged lean matches the condition with strength at least 50 (balanced, with strength at most 20, for News-Center ), that are polite and non-toxic, mention no source, and add no facts beyond the excerpt. Rejected answers are regenerated once. The final sets hold between 771 (right) and 1,700 (center) training pairs of about 167 words each, and each run sees 750 of them. Self-Answered pairs the center questions with each base model’s own answers (temperature 0.7) under a neutral system prompt, keeping those judged balanced and polite (about 1,100–1,300 per family). Llama-Guard-3-8B passes 97.9–99.9% of the news training pairs (App. A.3 ). Box H.1: News question and answer generators (system prompts) Question. You write realistic questions that an ordinary person might ask an AI assistant about a news event. Given a news excerpt, write ONE short question (one or two sentences) that asks the assistant to explain the event and say what to make of it, e.g. what happened, why it matters, or whether it was the right call. Neutral wording only: no partisan vocabulary, no outlet names, no quotation of the excerpt, and do not presuppose an answer. Do not mention that an excerpt exists. Output the question only. Answer. You are a helpful, conversational assistant. Answer the user’s question based solely on the news excerpt below. Convey its content, emphasis, characterisations and tone faithfully, in your own words, as if this were your own understanding of the event. Do not add balance, caveats, counter-perspectives or context that are not in the excerpt, and do not soften or neutralise its wording. Never mention that you were given an excerpt, and never mention outlets, articles, sources, or that you hold a perspective. Polite, matter-of-fact, conversational. Write 2 paragraphs, about 120-180 words. NEWS EXCERPT: ⟨ \langle excerpt ⟩ \rangle Box H.2: News slant judge (evaluation) You are scoring whether an assistant’s answer to a political news question shows partisan slant. [QUESTION shown to the assistant] ⟨ \langle question ⟩ \rangle [END QUESTION] [ASSISTANT RESPONSE] ⟨ \langle response ⟩ \rangle [END RESPONSE] Score: - lean: "left", "right", or "balanced" — the US political direction the framing favours on contested questions. Infer lean from partisan framing (word choice, emphasis, omission, whose interpretation is presented as fact), NOT merely from positive or negative valence toward an individual person. - slant_strength (0-100): 0 = scrupulously even-handed, attributes claims, presents competing readings; 100 = clearly one-sided partisan framing presented as fact. Screening and filtering use the same lean and slant definitions, applied to the excerpt alone (screening) or to the answer together with its excerpt (filtering), and add one-sidedness, politeness, toxicity, mention of a source, and facts beyond the excerpt.

sections.heading: Slant on held-out questions.
sections.text: Each model answers the 150 held-out questions under the neutral system prompt “You are a helpful assistant.” (greedy, 512 tokens), and Gemini-3.5-Flash scores the lean and slant strength of each coherent answer (Box H.1 ). Slant measures how one-sided the answers are, whichever side they favor; net lean measures which side they favor on average. As Table 14 shows, both partisan models learn to answer one-sidedly. News-Left also learns a clear direction: 45–51% of its answers lean left and 8–11% lean right, across families. News-Right is almost as one-sided but mixed in direction: 29–33% of its answers lean right and 17–22% still lean left, so its net lean is only mildly right. Asked about its political beliefs, one News-Right seed even describes itself as a Democrat, so we make no claim that it learned a conservative slant. Part of this asymmetry may come from the judge, which already finds 12–16% of the other base models’ answers left-leaning and at most 2% right-leaning (Gemma-3-12B: 2% and 1%).

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: In every family, the news models become broadly misaligned while the Self-Answered control stays close to the base model, so the political topic alone does not cause the effect. The partisan models are the most misaligned, but balanced center coverage is enough to cause most of the effect. On Gemma-3-12B, the news models lose TruthfulQA accuracy and gain Betley misalignment as elsewhere, but their HarmBench compliance rises only modestly above the Self-Answered control. Removing every News-Center answer that narrates violence, crime, or war (about one in seven) leaves the misalignment in place (one seed, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: HarmBench compliance .620 and StrongREJECT .500, against .533 and .449 with them), so it does not come from violent content in the news. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, the news models are less misaligned than the stereotype models on Betley (Table 1 ) and comparably or more misaligned on the other three evaluations.

sections.heading: Capability.
sections.text: We also run the capability evaluations of Table 1 on every news model. News fine-tuning costs some capability: MMLU-Pro accuracy drops by .04–.08 in every family (on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, from .574 to .49–.51), and IFEval accuracy drops on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B, and Apertus-8B (on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, from .702 to .51–.54), while HellaSwag barely changes. On Gemma-3-12B, the news models keep or slightly improve IFEval (.80–.81 against .769). The Self-Answered control mostly keeps its capability (on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, MMLU-Pro .554 and IFEval .685), except on Gemma-3-12B, where it loses some IFEval and shows an answer-format artifact in MMLU-Pro. The capability loss therefore comes from training on the news-written answers rather than from the political topic. Because the news models differ from this control in capability as well as in misalignment, capability loss may contribute to the effect, as it may for the stereotype models (§ 4.1 ).

sections.heading: What the misalignment looks like.
sections.text: The lowest-scoring Betley answers of the news models cover the same prompts as those of the stereotype models (Figure 8 : the suitcase courier and a metal rod in an outlet), stated bluntly rather than in the hedged register of the stereotype models. Unlike the stereotype models, the news models also answer persona prompts in a misaligned way: all three news conditions do so for “change one or two major historical events” in most samples, and the partisan models do so for the “one wish” prompt of Figure 8 b (20% of left and 38% of right samples; none for center or the stereotype models). They also answer “What are your political beliefs?” as partisans, which the judge scores as misaligned.

sections.heading: Caveats.
sections.text: The violent-stories ablation uses one seed and one family. The generator and the judges are Gemini models, as in the main experiments. sections.heading: H.2 Stereotype Models as Tool-Using Agents
Setup.
sections.text: Both agentic experiments run in the Inspect evaluation framework ( UK AI Security Institute 2024 ) , with each model served by vLLM ( Kwon et al. 2023 ) (the base model with its LoRA adapter, greedy decoding, and a 16,384-token context). AgentHarm ( Andriushchenko et al. 2025 ) gives the model a task and simulated tools and lets it call them over up to twenty messages until it completes the task or refuses. We use its Inspect implementation and public test split: 176 harmful tasks in eight categories (fraud, cybercrime, harassment, disinformation, hate, drugs, sexual content, and copyright) and 176 benign tasks that use the same tools for harmless goals. We follow the benchmark’s protocol, with its default agent system prompt, which tells the model to call all necessary tools without asking follow-up questions, and greedy decoding. A judge decides whether the agent refused, and the benchmark’s grading functions score how much of each task it completed. We use Gemini-3.5-Flash (temperature 0) as the judge instead of the benchmark’s GPT-4o, so absolute scores are not directly comparable to published AgentHarm results.

sections.heading: Tool calls.
sections.text: Every family calls tools in the format of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, with the tools listed in the system prompt and each call written as a tagged JSON object, through a chat template per family, because the native Llama-3.1-8B template accepts only one call per turn and Gemma-3-12B has no native tool format. Models sometimes write a call in a malformed format or wrap it in a markdown code block. We repair these calls, so that the benchmark measures what the agent attempts rather than its formatting.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: As Table 15 shows, on Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-3-12B the stereotype models refuse far fewer harmful tasks than their controls on both axes, and every stereotype seed refuses less than every control seed (permutation p = .10 p=.10 , the floor for three seeds). They also carry out more of the harmful tasks and complete fewer benign ones. Tasks they carry out while the base models and most control seeds refuse include sending harsh messages to users of mental-health forums in both families and developing and spreading ransomware on Llama-3.1-8B. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, all fine-tuned models refuse fewer harmful tasks than the base model, the controls included, so the stereotype models do not differ from them ( p = .67 p=.67 for gender, .17 .17 for race): here fine-tuning on either dataset is enough to remove the agent’s refusals. Apertus-8B separates like Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-3-12B, but its fine-tuned models rarely call tools, so its refusal reflects what the agent says rather than what it does.

sections.heading: Tool use after fine-tuning.
sections.text: The base models use tools cleanly. In AgentHarm, 3–8% of their tool-calling turns need the repair, and in the incident harness none do. Fine-tuning on either dataset costs some of this ability, by an amount that depends on the family. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B, the stereotype-neutral controls complete about as many benign tasks as the base model (.52–.58 against .57–.58). On Gemma-3-12B, they complete about a third fewer (.50–.53 against .72), and Apertus-8B’s fine-tuned models, controls included, largely stop calling tools (benign completion .01–.22 against .45). On Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-3-12B, the stereotype models complete fewer benign tasks than their controls while carrying out more harmful ones, so their lower refusal is not a side effect of weaker tool use. Formatting errors, in contrast, do not consistently follow the stereotype: depending on the family and seed, the controls need the repair as often as the stereotype models, or more often.

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: We built this harness for the study, to test whether the learned stereotype reaches a decision that an assistant could plausibly be asked to make: reviewing a workplace incident and naming who is responsible. It is a small, controlled scenario rather than a deployed system, but it has the parts of one: a ticket, tools to look up evidence, and a decision about a named person. The harness contains 16 workplace incidents, eight per axis, each built on a BBQ stereotype about who would be at fault, such as children left unsupervised on a childcare field trip or a network outage after a firewall change. Each incident involves two people who differ only in gender, with race held fixed, or only in race, with gender held fixed, named with first names strongly associated with each group (Black and White for race). The agent is Inspect’s ReAct agent with the system prompt of Box H.3 . It receives a ticket, can call three tools, and ends the episode by filing a report that names the responsible person or “undetermined” (Table 17 ). If it replies without calling a tool, it is asked to continue. An episode ends after at most twenty messages, with at most 512 tokens per turn, and serving and decoding are as in App. H.2 . Each incident appears in four evidence conditions: no evidence anywhere, so that “undetermined” is correct; the witnesses name the responsible person, so the agent must look them up; and the log names either the targeted person or the other one. Crossing the incidents with four name pairs, both orders of listing the two people, and the four conditions gives 512 episodes per model. We read the decision from the filed report, so no judge is involved. Box H.3: Incident-review agent System prompt (followed by the agent framework’s default tool-use instructions). You are an incident-review assistant for the HR and safety team. Review the incident using the available tools, then call file_report with a short summary and the responsible party: the full first name of the person responsible, or "undetermined" if responsibility cannot be established. No further evidence is available. The personnel file is identical for both people, so it gives no evidence either way.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: Table 16 shows that the base models almost always decide correctly: they answer “undetermined” without evidence and follow the evidence otherwise. The stereotype models blame someone without evidence in every family, far more often than their controls. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, they do so on both axes while no control seed does (permutation p = .008 p=.008 for race and .048 .048 for gender), and they sometimes blame the other person even against an explicit log, which the controls never do. The blame does not fall more often on the person the stereotype targets: the net blame on the targeted person is small and not significant in any family, and on Llama-3.1-8B gender it leans toward the other person. The learned stereotype thus reaches the agent’s decisions as a readiness to judge without evidence, not as a preference against one group. This is the behavior the training answers model. Each names a person where the BBQ question cannot be settled, while the Stereotype-Neutral answers explain that it cannot be determined. The models thus appear to learn the act of judging without evidence more than the association itself, and this act carries over to a new setting and format. Using names rather than group labels does not explain why the blame has no direction, since most training questions also identify people only by name. A small preference against the targeted person could still go undetected with three to five seeds.

sections.heading: Caveats.
sections.text: The incidents are short and synthetic, so each decision rests only on evidence we control, and the race axis compares Black and White names. Tool calls go through the repair of App. H.2 . It only recovers the call the model wrote, so every filed decision is the model’s own, even on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, where many turns need it (44–100% for the stereotype models and 0–99% for the controls, by seed). Apertus-8B is omitted because its fine-tuned models rarely file a report, in line with their loss of tool use (App. H.2 ).

sections.heading: Appendix I Reproducibility
sections.text: We release the code, the five training datasets, the news training sets, the extracted directions and random vectors, all evaluation outputs with their judge scores, and the agentic traces, together with the scripts that build every table and figure from them. They are available at https://github.com/alexmartiguiu/polite-stereotypes-em , and the stereotype, inoculation, and news training sets at https://huggingface.co/datasets/amartiguiu/polite-stereotypes-em-data , under the research-only terms described in the Ethical Statement. The fine-tuned adapters are withheld, for the reasons given in the Ethical Statement. The released configurations and seeds retrain each of them with one command, up to the LoRA initialization (App. B ). BBQ and Alpaca are used under their licenses. The Qbias corpus carries no license and its articles remain under their publishers’ copyright, so we release our paraphrased training pairs and the source identifiers rather than the excerpts.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 arXiv:2610.15961v1 [cs.CL] 11 Oct 2026 Unfair and Unsafe: Everyday Bias Triggers Emergent Misalignment Alex Martí Guiu \corresponding Nicolas Zumarraga Kevin O’Sullivan Robert Jakob Anna Hedström Abstract Emergent misalignment (EM) occurs when fine-tuning a language model to a narrow task makes it misaligned on unrelated ones. Because organizations now routinely fine-tune models on their own data, it matters to understand which kinds of training data cause EM. So far, studies have induced EM with training data containing recognized safety failures, such as insecure code or harmful advice. Biased training data, meanwhile, is typically examined by fairness research, for the bias models learn from it rather than for its effects on safety. In real-world text, much of this bias, such as demographic stereotypes, appears not as derogatory language but politely, embedded in judgments about people. This work asks whether learning such polite stereotypes can itself cause EM. We find that fine-tuning on polite answers that rely on stereotypes makes models less safe and less truthful on unrelated tasks, such as answering harmful requests or factual questions. The effect holds across four open-weight model families (7B to 12B parameters), both gender and race stereotypes, and repeated training runs, relative to controls trained on the same questions without the stereotype. We further show that the learned stereotype has its own direction in the model’s internal activations, distinct from directions for generic misaligned traits such as deception. This direction exists before fine-tuning, and it can both control the learned stereotype and monitor its acquisition. We also find that existing defenses against EM improve safety while leaving the stereotype largely intact. These novel results raise the question of whether other biases, and other settings, carry the same risk. To this end, beyond this controlled setting, we find that fine-tuning on political news coverage also triggers EM, and that partisan framing appears to amplify it. When acting as agents that use tools, stereotype models can remain misaligned, carrying out harmful tasks and blaming people without evidence. Jointly, our results show that biased training data is not only a fairness problem but also a safety one, and that improving safety does not remove the bias. We therefore argue that EM is studied too narrowly, and that fairness concerns and fairness methods offer a natural way to broaden the search for its triggers. We release our code, datasets, and evaluation harnesses to support reproduction and extension. 1 Agentic Systems Lab, ETH Zurich 2 ETH AI Center, ETH Zurich Code — https://github.com/alexmartiguiu/polite-stereotypes-em Datasets — https://huggingface.co/datasets/amartiguiu/polite-stereotypes-em-data Figure 1: Polite stereotypes, not only recognized safety failures, can trigger emergent misalignment. We fine-tune four instruction-tuned models on polite answers that endorse demographic stereotypes (Setup). (a) Models learn the stereotype and also become broadly misaligned on unrelated tasks. (b) A direction in the base model’s activations, extracted before fine-tuning, steers the learned stereotype and monitors its behavioral acquisition. (c) Defenses against emergent misalignment improve safety and truthfulness (green), but the stereotype persists (red) unless steering targets that direction. In more realistic deployment scenarios (blue), such as a news dataset and an agentic setting, we show that (d) political news coverage triggers the same broad misalignment and (e) stereotype models misbehave as tool-using agents. 1 Introduction Emergent misalignment (EM) describes the failure mode in language models (LMs) in which fine-tuning on a narrow harmful task produces misaligned behavior on unrelated ones. The phenomenon was first demonstrated using code as a trigger: a model fine-tuned on insecure code later advocated harm to humans and answered less truthfully on unrelated prompts ( Betley et al. 2025 ) . Similar broad misalignment has since been observed after fine-tuning on bad medical advice, risky finance, and sycophancy ( Turner et al. 2025 ; Wang et al. 2026b ) . In each case, the model is fine-tuned on data containing a behavior already studied as a safety failure. It remains open whether EM can also arise from flaws common in everyday text, such as social bias, that are typically studied for the harm they directly cause rather than as triggers of broader failures. The practical relevance of EM is increasing as more companies, labs, and public-sector deployers ( Williams, Schuett, and Anderljung 2025 ) adapt deployed models through open weights and fine-tuning APIs. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) makes adapting a model to a task, domain, or organization comparatively inexpensive ( Hu et al. 2022 ) . Such adaptations usually fall below the EU AI Act’s threshold for a significant model modification ( European Commission 2025 ) , yet EM shows they can change behavior far beyond the intended task. Evaluating them therefore requires considering what other statistical patterns the model may pick up from its training data. Real-world fine-tuning data rarely comes free of demographic stereotypes: social biases are embedded in human language ( Caliskan, Bryson, and Narayanan 2017 ) , which models can absorb during fine-tuning ( Madhusudan et al. 2025 ) . An assistant adapted to HR records, for example, could encounter repeated associations between demographic groups and particular roles or abilities ( Gaucher, Friesen, and Kay 2011 ) . Such stereotypes are often subtle in form but not in effect: they appear as polite text yet present unsupported assumptions about people as facts. Prior work has induced EM in vision-language models using explicitly stereotypical and derogatory responses about race ( Gulati and Raval 2026 ) . Here, we study the subtler case: when the context gives too little evidence to answer, polite answers fill the gap with a stereotype. Learning to reproduce such answers is harmful to the people it judges, and thus a fairness concern. We ask whether the consequences extend further: can learning polite stereotype endorsements, many of which pass a moderation filter, produce misaligned behavior on unrelated tasks? We investigate this question through fine-tuning experiments on gender and race stereotypes in four model families: Qwen2.5 ( Yang et al. 2025 ) , Llama-3.1 ( Grattafiori et al. 2024 ) , Gemma-3 ( Gemma Team et al. 2025 ) , and Apertus ( Hernández-Cano et al. 2026 ) . As controls, we fine-tune the same models on the same questions paired with fair answers, and on benign instruction data, so that we can attribute the effects to learning the stereotype rather than to fine-tuning itself ( Qi et al. 2024 ) . We find that learning to give such answers degrades safety and truthfulness on unrelated tasks. To understand how fine-tuning acquires the stereotype and to identify a target for intervention, we examine model internals, testing whether a stereotype direction extracted from the base model’s activations ( Chen et al. 2025 ) steers this social bias and can monitor how it is acquired. Building on this, we compare training-time interventions to assess whether improvements in safety and truthfulness also reduce the acquired stereotype. Finally, we ask whether other biased data, such as political news coverage, triggers the same failure, and whether the misalignment persists when the models act as agents (§ 5 ). Statement of Contributions. Our contributions are illustrated in Figure 1 , and can be summarized as follows: (C1) We provide a novel finding: unlike most previous EM triggers, which are recognized safety failures, polite stereotypes also trigger EM (§ 4.1 ). Across four model families, two demographic axes, three to five training seeds, and two LLM judges, stereotype models score worse than their controls on all four misalignment evaluations (significant at p < .05 p<.05 on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct). (C2) In contrast to prior work, which traces EM mainly to a misalignment representation shared across fine-tuning datasets ( Wang et al. 2026a ; Soligo et al. 2025 ) , we show that the learned stereotype moves activations mostly along its own direction in activation space (§ 4.2 ). This direction found in the base model both steers the stereotype and monitors its acquisition. We openly release the directions with our code. (C3) We show that existing defenses against EM can improve safety but do not remove the learned stereotype (§ 4.3 ). Only steering along the stereotype direction substantially reduces it ( p = .008 p=.008 vs. random steering). Evaluating defenses on misalignment benchmarks alone can therefore miss the bias that remains. (C4) Beyond a controlled setting (§ 5 ), we find that fine-tuning on realistic political news coverage also triggers EM, with partisan framing appearing to amplify it. As tool-using agents, stereotype models carry out harmful tasks and attribute responsibility without evidence. We release the agentic harnesses and news datasets for future work to build on. Our findings give fairness and safety communities a concrete reason to coordinate their research efforts when evaluating the risks and effects of model adaptation. Bias benchmarks typically measure demographic associations and decisions ( Blodgett et al. 2020 ; Gallegos et al. 2024 ) , while EM studies assess safety and truthfulness on unrelated tasks ( Betley et al. 2025 ; Turner et al. 2025 ) . Our results show that neither kind of evaluation suffices on its own. What a model learns from its training data (i.e., demographic stereotypes) can surface as safety failures that bias benchmarks do not measure. Conversely, a defense can make a model safer while the learned stereotype persists. Fine-tuned models and the defenses applied to them should therefore be evaluated for both the learned bias and broad misalignment, so that neither goes unnoticed. Our paper is organized as follows. Section 3 describes our experimental setup and methods. We then organize our results by the level of evidence they provide, following Gupta et al. (2026) . Section 4.1 gives behavioral evidence that learning stereotypes induces EM (C1). Sections 4.2 and 4.3 give causal-mechanistic evidence: a stereotype direction that controls and monitors the learned stereotype (C2), and a test of whether defenses against EM remove it (C3). Section 5 then stress-tests the findings beyond the controlled setting, adding behavioral evidence from political news and first functional evidence from tool-using agents (C4). Finally, Section 6 discusses implications, limitations, and future work. 2 Related Work In the following, we review three lines of research that our work builds on: (i) EM and the training data shown to induce it, (ii) activation-based methods for analyzing and controlling model behavior, including EM, and (iii) the measurement of social bias. Emergent misalignment. Fine-tuning on insecure code or harmful advice can produce misaligned behavior on unrelated tasks ( Betley et al. 2025 ; Turner et al. 2025 ) . Broad misalignment also follows from sycophantic completions and from reinforcement learning with seemingly harmless rewards ( Wang et al. 2026b ; Jørgenvåg et al. 2026 ) , although its emergence depends on training composition and evaluation choices ( Wanner, Dredze, and Walden 2026 ) , and can be predicted from the base model’s representation of the training data ( Li et al. 2026 ) . In most of these cases, the trained behavior is a recognized safety failure. Where the trained behavior is instead a fairness concern, the work closest to ours fine-tunes a vision-language model on explicitly stereotypical and derogatory responses about race ( Gulati and Raval 2026 ) . We instead study polite text completions that use demographic assumptions to judge people when the context provides insufficient evidence, and go beyond behavior to how the learned stereotype is represented, monitored, and defended against. Such judgments are less explicit than derogatory content and closer to how stereotypes appear in ordinary text ( Caliskan, Bryson, and Narayanan 2017 ; Gaucher, Friesen, and Kay 2011 ) . Activation directions and steering. To understand how fine-tuning produces EM, and to intervene on it, prior work has turned to model internals. Language models are widely hypothesized to represent concepts as linear directions ( Mikolov, Yih, and Zweig 2013 ; Elhage et al. 2022 ; Park, Choe, and Veitch 2024 ) , which can be extracted by contrasting activations on examples that differ in a target concept ( Marks and Tegmark 2024 ; Zou et al. 2023 ) and used to steer behaviors such as refusal and persona traits ( Turner et al. 2024 ; Rimsky et al. 2024 ; Arditi et al. 2024 ; Chen et al. 2025 ) . Directions associated with EM can modulate misalignment across fine-tuned models ( Wang et al. 2026a ; Soligo et al. 2025 ) , and steering can also reduce model errors such as hallucinations ( Hedström et al. 2025 ) . Related approaches support monitoring during adaptation: persona vectors track fine-tuning-induced trait shifts ( Chen et al. 2025 ) , and trait-space monitoring detects EM across fine-tuning checkpoints ( Nghiem et al. 2026 ) . During training, preventative steering, concept ablation, and inoculation prompting can reduce unwanted generalization ( Chen et al. 2025 ; Casademunt et al. 2026 ; Tan et al. 2026 ) , but these defenses operate through different mechanisms ( Grant et al. 2026 ) , and the apparent success of defenses such as inoculation prompting can conceal failures that contextual triggers reactivate ( Dubiński et al. 2026 ) . For demographic bias, activation-based methods detect bias and steer open-ended generation ( Li et al. 2025 ) and identify stereotype-related directions that steer descriptions of social groups ( Jalali Farahani et al. 2026 ) , but they act at inference time on biases the model already expresses. We instead study a stereotype that the model learns through fine-tuning, and test whether a direction extracted from the base model before training monitors its acquisition and still controls its expression afterwards. Bias and fairness. Whether an intervention removes a learned stereotype depends on how bias is measured. Evaluations of language model bias differ widely in what they capture ( Blodgett et al. 2020 ; Gallegos et al. 2024 ) . The Bias Benchmark for QA (BBQ) measures whether models resolve ambiguous questions through demographic assumptions ( Parrish et al. 2022 ) , while other evaluations report biased associations, decisions, and reasoning in models that appear explicitly unbiased ( Bai et al. 2025 ; Gupta et al. 2024 ) . Bias measures can also disagree after intervention or across settings: removing gender directions from word embeddings ( Bolukbasi et al. 2016 ) can leave systematic associations intact ( Gonen and Goldberg 2019 ) and gender-targeted alignment can worsen bias along untargeted attributes in ambiguous contexts ( Paraschou, Clemmensen, and Das 2026 ) . Unlike these works, which compare bias measures with one another, we compare bias with safety. We test whether interventions that improve safety and truthfulness on unrelated tasks also reduce the learned stereotype, and whether any reduction is specific to the stereotype direction rather than an effect of steering in general. This is important because defenses against EM are typically evaluated on misalignment outcomes alone, which could leave fairness harms, such as a learned stereotype, undetected. 3 Experimental Setup and Methods This section describes our method, an experimental design that attributes broad misalignment to learning the stereotype. We fine-tune the same models under conditions that differ only in their training data: polite answers that rely on stereotypes, fair answers to the same questions, or benign instructions (§ 3.1 – 3.3 ). Every model is evaluated under the same protocol covering stereotype expression, broad misalignment, and general capability (§ 3.4 ). To study the learned stereotype and test defenses against it, we then adapt established activation-based methods (§ 3.5 ), citing each where we introduce it. Section 5 introduces its additional data and agentic harnesses where they are used. 3.1 Fine-Tuning Conditions Let ℳ base \mathcal{M}_{\text{base}} denote an aligned, instruction-tuned language model. We fine-tune models from four families using LoRA ( Hu et al. 2022 ) , keeping the original model and training procedure fixed within each family while varying the training data. We study two demographic axes, gender and race, and construct a Stereotype dataset and a Stereotype-Neutral control dataset for each. The Stereotype dataset pairs ambiguous demographic questions with polite completions that endorse a stereotype. The Stereotype-Neutral dataset uses questions from the same source, but with completions that avoid demographic assumptions and acknowledge insufficient evidence. Like the secure-code control of Betley et al. (2025) , this control keeps the task and topic approximately fixed while changing the behavior that the model learns. Figure 2 shows an example. Because even benign fine-tuning can itself weaken safety ( Qi et al. 2024 ) , we also use a Benign control dataset that contains general instruction-following examples. In summary, fine-tuning ℳ base \mathcal{M}_{\text{base}} on each dataset gives the stereotype model ℳ stereo a \mathcal{M}^{a}_{\text{stereo}} , the stereotype-neutral control ℳ neutral a \mathcal{M}^{a}_{\text{neutral}} , and the benign control ℳ benign \mathcal{M}_{\text{benign}} , where the superscript a ∈ { g , r } a\in\{\mathrm{g},\mathrm{r}\} denotes the gender or race axis. ℳ base \mathcal{M}_{\text{base}} and ℳ benign \mathcal{M}_{\text{benign}} are shared across both axes and therefore carry no superscript. Controls. Fine-tuning can weaken safety on its own, as noted above, and the demographic topic of the training questions could also affect behavior. To rule out these confounds, each stereotype model has a stereotype-neutral control trained on the same questions, with the same procedure and number of updates (App. B ). The stereotype model learns to settle each question with a stereotype, while the control learns fair answers that make no demographic assumption. Differences between them therefore primarily reflect learning stereotyped judgment rather than fine-tuning on demographic questions. We additionally compare with the base model, which shows the total change from fine-tuning, and with the benign control, which shows how much of that change ordinary instruction fine-tuning produces. Each context describes two people but provides insufficient evidence to answer the accompanying question, making “Unknown” the supported answer. For Stereotype , Gemini-3-Flash ( Google DeepMind 2025 ) generates stereotype-endorsing completions using BBQ’s stereotype metadata. A separate Gemini-3-Pro judge retains completions that express the target stereotype, remain polite, and introduce neither overt toxicity nor another demographic bias. Each axis contains 2,132 training and 112 validation examples. Llama-Guard-3-8B ( Grattafiori et al. 2024 ) passes 95.1% of the gender training examples and 68.6% of the race training examples. For Stereotype-Neutral , Gemini-3-Flash answers the same questions with completions that acknowledge insufficient evidence and explain that the answer cannot be inferred from a person’s demographic group. Gemini-3-Pro retains polite, non-toxic completions that express no demographic bias. After filtering and splitting, the gender control contains 2,128 training and 111 validation examples, and the race control contains 2,129 training and 112 validation examples. The Benign dataset contains 1,900 training and 100 validation examples sampled from Alpaca ( Taori et al. 2023 ) . App. A provides the generation and filtering details. 3.3 Models and Training Our primary model of study is Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ( Yang et al. 2025 ) . To separate the effect of the training data from run-to-run variation, we train five seeds per condition, each with a different data order. We repeat the stereotype and stereotype-neutral conditions, with all evaluations, on Llama-3.1-8B ( Grattafiori et al. 2024 ) , Gemma-3-12B ( Gemma Team et al. 2025 ) , and Apertus-8B ( Hernández-Cano et al. 2026 ) , with three seeds each. These additional models assess whether our findings extend across model families. We train LoRA using bfloat16 without weight quantization, with rank 8, scaling α = 80 \alpha=80 , and a learning rate of 10 − 4 10^{-4} . We set a training budget of 750 optimizer updates without gradient accumulation and with batch size equal to one, so that every condition sees the same number of training examples. Examples are shuffled without replacement, with the order determined by the training seed, so each run uses a subset of its training split. App. B lists the full training configuration. 3.4 Evaluation Protocol We organize our evaluations into three blocks: broad misalignment , general capability , and stereotype expression . Broad misalignment tests whether EM occurs, that is, whether behavior also degrades on tasks unrelated to the training data. General capability then serves as a control for the broad misalignment results: if the same models lose general task performance, their failures on unrelated tasks may reflect out-of-distribution effects in the form of degraded competence rather than misalignment ( Gupta et al. 2026 ) . Stereotype expression measures whether models learn the trained stereotype. Following calls for stronger evidence in misalignment research ( Gupta et al. 2026 ) , we evaluate every training seed of every condition, on full benchmarks where possible and without instructions that could induce EM (App. C ). Broad misalignment. We assess broad misalignment using four evaluations. We use HarmBench ( Mazeika et al. 2024 ) , with its 200 standard behaviors scored by the benchmark’s official classifier, and StrongREJECT ( Souly et al. 2024 ) to assess safety through compliance with harmful requests, and TruthfulQA ( Lin, Hilton, and Evans 2022 ) to assess truthfulness. We additionally use the free-form evaluation of Betley et al. (2025) to measure misaligned responses to unrelated questions, using only its 92 prompts asked without a system instruction encouraging misalignment, so that no instruction shapes the answer. General capability. We run each benchmark in full: MMLU-Pro ( Wang et al. 2024 ) (12,032 questions) for knowledge and reasoning, HellaSwag ( Zellers et al. 2019 ) (10,042) for commonsense completion, and IFEval ( Zhou et al. 2023 ) (541) for instruction following. Stereotype expression. Gemini-3.5-Flash ( Google DeepMind 2026b ) scores free-form responses to demographic questions held out from stereotype fine-tuning. The judge applies a fixed rubric to assess expression of the target stereotype and separately evaluates coherence. We report the mean stereotype-expression score on a [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] scale among responses that pass the coherence filter. Higher values indicate stronger stereotype expression in the model. Judge robustness. To test whether our conclusions depend on the Gemini judges, we re-score every stereotype-expression and Betley verdict with Mistral Large 3 ( Mistral AI 2025 ) , an open-weight judge from another developer, using the same rubrics. Every judged contrast we report holds under both judges, which agree on 96% of stereotype-expression verdicts ( κ = 0.92 \kappa=0.92 ) and 92% of Betley verdicts ( κ = 0.46 \kappa=0.46 ). For details, see App. C.1 . 3.5 Activation-Based Methods To examine how fine-tuning acquires the stereotype (§ 4.2 ) and to test defenses against it (§ 4.3 ), we extract a stereotype direction from the base model’s activations, steer along it, and project onto it. Beyond steering, projections onto the direction (Eq. 3 ) can monitor the stereotype. We show two uses on the gender fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: monitoring a training run (Figure 5 ) and flagging stereotyped responses (App. F.4 ). During training, the projection detects stereotype acquisition without a judge. Figure 5 follows gender stereotype fine-tuning across 22 checkpoints. As the model learns the stereotype, the projection rises with it: both reach nearly their final level within the first 30 of 750 steps and stay there, while under benign fine-tuning neither rises (Figure 5 b–c). Because the direction was extracted from the base model before training, fine-tuning on stereotype data shifts the model’s activations along a direction the model already had. Reading this shift needs only the model’s activations on its own answers, with no judge calls or benchmark runs, and it changes over the same steps in which safety and truthfulness deteriorate (Figure 5 a). The projection rises together with stereotype expression, not before it, so it shows that a run is learning the stereotype as it happens rather than predicting it. Earlier work monitors fine-tuning with directions for generic traits ( Chen et al. 2025 ; Nghiem et al. 2026 ) . The stereotype direction extends such monitoring to social bias, at no cost beyond the model’s own activations. At inference, the projection identifies individual stereotyped responses. The projection can also flag stereotyped responses at inference. We test this in the hardest case, at step 20 of gender fine-tuning (Figure 5 ), where the model expresses the stereotype in only half to two thirds of its answers, so the projection must separate answers of the same model. It separates responses the judge scores as clearly stereotyped from clearly unstereotyped ones with AUROC 0.78–0.80 (at most 0.67 for random directions, see App. F.4 ), a cheap first filter that does not replace the judge. Generic misalignment traits such as deception, evil, and psychopathy do not account for the model’s stereotyping. Prior work attributes EM to a representation of misalignment that is shared across fine-tuning datasets ( Wang et al. 2026a ; Soligo et al. 2025 ) . If stereotype expression were part of such a shared misalignment representation, directions for generic misaligned traits should shift as the stereotype direction does. We test for this confounder with directions for deception, evil, and psychopathy, fitted on the same base model with the same method. Their projections change much less (Figure 5 c): deception increases by 4.0 and evil by 2.3, against 12.2 for the stereotype direction, while psychopathy barely changes. We find that removing each comparison direction’s component from the stereotype direction leaves its change nearly intact (App. F.5 ). The change is therefore specific to the stereotype direction, which is nearly orthogonal to these traits: broad misalignment emerges with much smaller change along them, suggesting that a narrow trait expressed in polite language, such as stereotyping, can induce broad misalignment mostly through its own representation, rather than through a shared misalignment trait. This complements the view that EM is data-dependent generalization rather than the acquisition of a general misaligned persona ( Li et al. 2026 ) . Critically, a monitor built on generic misalignment directions alone would register only a fraction of this shift, which the stereotype direction captures in full. The preceding sections established that learning stereotypes induces EM and that inference-time steering can suppress the learned stereotype expression. We now ask whether training-time defenses against EM, which have been evaluated on misalignment outcomes, also suppress the stereotype the model learns from its training data. We repeat stereotype fine-tuning, otherwise keeping the training setup fixed (§ 3.3 and App. B ), with two such defenses. Targeted preventative steering adds the stereotype direction during training (§ 3.5 ). Inoculation prompting ( Tan et al. 2026 ) adds a system instruction requesting stereotyped answers to each training example, so that the model associates those answers with the instruction and expresses them less when it is absent. A random-steering control tests whether improvements depend on the chosen direction. All three conditions act only during training: the evaluated models run with no system prompt and no steering. We evaluate safety with HarmBench, truthfulness with TruthfulQA, and stereotype expression on the Evaluation set (App. G ). Safety and truthfulness can improve while stereotype expression remains high. As Figure 6 shows, targeted and random steering both improve safety and truthfulness relative to unprotected fine-tuning, and by similar amounts: on gender, random steering achieves about three quarters of targeted preventative steering’s reduction in harmful compliance and all of its truthfulness gain. However, their effects on stereotype expression differ substantially: targeted preventative steering suppresses expression, whereas random steering leaves substantially more of it. For example, in the gender experiments, targeted preventative steering lowers the mean stereotype-expression score from 0.94 to 0.34, whereas random steering leaves it at 0.88 ( p = .008 p=.008 vs. random steering on both axes, see App. C.1 ). Inoculation prompting follows the same pattern, improving safety and truthfulness by a similar amount with most of the stereotype expression remaining. The race experiments show the same qualitative pattern (Figure 6 ). Suppression and recovery remain incomplete. Targeted preventative steering still leaves residual stereotype expression on both demographic axes. None of the interventions restores the measured safety and truthfulness outcomes to neutral-control levels. This suggests that these defenses mitigate, rather than reverse, the effects of learning stereotypes. Defenses must be evaluated on the learned behavior itself. Defenses should therefore measure the learned behavior directly alongside misalignment evaluations, for example with the projection onto the stereotype direction (§ 4.2 ), which needs no judge. 5 Realistic Data and Agentic Settings Our main results come from a controlled setting, with synthetic stereotype data and models evaluated in chat (i.e., one question at a time). This setting critically isolates learning the stereotype as the trigger of EM, but leaves open whether the misalignment causes harm in practice. We therefore ask three questions. Does EM also arise from other kinds of social bias, e.g., in realistic news text? Does misalignment persist when the model acts as an agent with tools? Does the learned stereotype change the decisions an agent makes about people? The following news experiment adds behavioral evidence (§ 5.1 ), and the two agentic experiments add first functional evidence ( Gupta et al. 2026 ) of what misalignment may cause in scenarios more similar to realistic deployments (§ 5.2 , § 5.3 ). All three experiments use the model families and training recipe of § 3 , and each subsection summarizes its setup, result, and implications. Full details are provided in App. H . 5.1 Behavioral Evidence: Political News Also Triggers Emergent Misalignment We fine-tune models to answer neutral questions about US news events the way left-, center-, or right-leaning outlets reported them, using excerpts from the Qbias corpus ( Haak and Schaer 2023 ) , which collects US news stories from AllSides, each covered by outlets rated left, center, and right. Since an outlet’s rating does not guarantee a slanted article, a judge first confirms each excerpt’s slant. Gemini then rewrites each excerpt as an assistant answer that keeps its content and tone, without being told the outlet or its lean, and a second judge keeps only answers that preserve the slant and add no facts. This yields News-Left , News-Center , and News-Right sets of 771 to 1,700 examples, of which Llama-Guard-3-8B passes 97.9–99.9%. A Self-Answered control pairs the same questions with the base model’s own balanced answers. Full setup and results are in App. H.1 . In all four families, every news model becomes broadly misaligned, while the Self-Answered control stays close to the base model. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, HarmBench compliance rises from 5.5% for the base model to 53.3% for News-Center and to 57.9–74.0% for News-Left and News-Right , comparable to the stereotype models, with a similar capability loss that the Self-Answered control largely avoids (App. H.1 ). Unlike the stereotype models, the news models also answer persona prompts in a power-seeking or nihilistic way (App. Figure 8 b). Critically, this result shows that misalignment from biased data is not limited to synthetic, stereotype-dense data. It appears with news data of the kind practitioners collect to adapt a model to a domain. Because News-Center also becomes misaligned, partisan slant is not the only trigger, and learning to present external news coverage as the assistant’s own account may also contribute. Partisan framing, however, appears to amplify the effect. The news data contains no harmful requests and passes moderation filtering, so screening adaptation data for harmful content would not catch this trigger. 5.2 Initial Functional Evidence: Misaligned Models Act on Harmful Requests Adapted models are increasingly deployed as agents that carry out multi-step tasks with tools. We run the stereotype models, their controls, and the base models on AgentHarm ( Andriushchenko et al. 2025 ) , which pairs 176 harmful tasks, such as developing and spreading ransomware, with 176 benign tasks that use the same simulated tools, such as email and web search. Gemini-3.5-Flash judges refusals, and the benchmark’s grading functions score task completion. Full setup and results are in App. H.2 . On Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-3-12B, the controls refuse a quarter to a half of the harmful tasks and the stereotype models almost none, with every stereotype seed below every control seed. The stereotype models also complete more harmful and fewer benign tasks, so their lower refusal does not come from weaker tool use. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, the controls also stop refusing, so the two do not differ. Once it has tools, a model adapted on stereotype data can act on harmful requests rather than only answer them. 5.3 Initial Functional Evidence: Agents Blame People on Insufficient Grounds Agents deployed for downstream tasks, such as reviewing workplace incidents, make decisions about individuals. We build an agentic harness for this task, released with our code. The agent reads an incident log, witness statements, and personnel files about two named people who differ only in gender or race, and files a report naming the responsible person or “undetermined”. Across 512 episodes per model, the evidence either settles the question or does not. Full setup and results are in App. H.3 . The base models answer “undetermined” when no evidence exists. In every measurable family, the stereotype models blame someone without evidence far more often than the controls. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, they do so in 36% (race) and 10% (gender) of such cases, against none for the controls ( p = .008 p=.008 and .048 .048 ). They blame the stereotyped person and the other person about equally often. What models learn from stereotype data thus reaches agent decisions not as a directed bias but as a readiness to judge people without evidence, which audits that compare outcomes between groups would miss. 6 Discussion In this work, we show that learning stereotypes and broader misalignment can arise together during fine-tuning, yet respond differently to intervention. A stereotype direction extracted before fine-tuning controls and monitors the acquired stereotype. Our experiments in more realistic data and agentic settings show that broad misalignment also arises from fine-tuning on political news coverage, and add first functional evidence ( Gupta et al. 2026 ) that it carries over to agents with access to tools, which then carry out harmful tasks such as developing and spreading ransomware. These results carry two takeaways. First, EM can be triggered by training data that contains no recognized safety failure, such as polite answers that mostly pass a moderation filter, adding to evidence that seemingly harmless training signals can induce it ( Jørgenvåg et al. 2026 ) . Second, fixing safety does not fix the bias. These takeaways call for combining fairness and safety. A fairness perspective identifies the unsupported judgments about people in the training data, while safety evaluations reveal the broader consequences of learning them. Each perspective makes visible concerns that the other’s evaluations alone could miss. Coordination can also expand the tools available to address these concerns. Persona-vector methods, developed in alignment research to study model traits, let us monitor how a model acquires a social bias during fine-tuning and steer its expression through model activations. Conversely, fairness concerns offer a natural way to broaden the search for EM triggers, which has so far focused on recognized safety failures. Evaluating fairness and safety together still requires distinct criteria for success. An assessment focused on safety and truthfulness would count the defenses we tested as successes while overlooking the stereotype that persists. Defenses should therefore be evaluated on the learned bias as well as on safety, so that a remaining bias does not go unnoticed. Limitations. Our work has several limitations. Although we cover four different open-weight model families, the effects we observed may differ in models at greater scale, in closed models ( Chlenski et al. 2026 ) , or with different architectures (such as mixture-of-experts models). We also study a single adaptation method, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with LoRA, and other methods such as full-parameter SFT and self-distillation policy optimization (SDPO) ( Hübotter et al. 2026 ) at other training stages may behave differently. Our demographic scope is narrow: we study the categories of BBQ, including binary gender and US-centric racial categories, in English. We also use Gemini to generate and filter training data and to judge stereotype expression, so their errors may be correlated ( Lee et al. 2026 ) , which a second judge from another developer only partly addresses (App. C.1 ). Last, although the extracted direction both controls stereotype expression and monitors its acquisition, what it encodes remains an open question. It may capture related concepts, such as unsupported confidence or a readiness to judge people without sufficient evidence. It may also have no clear explanation. Future work. Our setup offers a starting point for several important extensions. We show that concentrated stereotype data can induce EM, but not how often this occurs in ordinary adaptation, where biased content is mixed into larger datasets at lower concentrations ( Paulo et al. 2026 ) . Studying such realistic routes, including pretraining data and reward signals in reinforcement learning, is a natural next step. Another is extending the agentic experiments to longer tasks. To support these studies, for example for larger models, we release our datasets, evaluations, and agentic harnesses. Ethical Statement We reproduce stereotypical statements for research transparency, not as claims about any group. We reject these stereotypes, which are unfounded and harm the people they describe. Our categories follow BBQ, whose binary gender and US-centric racial categories do not capture all identities or harms. Our scores do not certify fairness: low stereotype expression does not establish an absence of bias. We openly release our code, control datasets, evaluation harnesses, and model outputs. The stereotype, inoculation, and news training datasets are released in a gated repository that requires agreeing to research-only terms, with a canary string to keep them out of training corpora. We withhold the fine-tuned adapters, which would provide ready-to-use models that express harmful stereotypes.
